title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Deck and fence maintenance
audience: Deck and fence maintenance owners who want more planned work from strata and body corporate managers, property managers, holiday rental managers and public bodies in their service area.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Identify public signals that a deck or fence need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the deck and fence work you do well, such as seasonal maintenance of common-area decks and boundary fences, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, the job sizes you can sustain, and how often each kind of client needs you. A fortnightly or seasonal round on a route you already run is usually worth more than a single large job across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column, a status column, a source and a date added. Score each as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. Ask whether the prospect sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat maintenance need, whether you can reach the decision-maker, and whether the work sits inside your licence and insurance. Strata and body corporate managers with common-area decks and fences, property managers, and holiday rental managers are candidates to test. The research did not find evidence of how often these groups buy deck or fence maintenance, so treat each group as a hypothesis. Use only business contact details published for business use. A business address is not automatically open to marketing.

instruction.heading: Watch public signals
instruction.body: In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders, lets suppliers set alerts, and publishes each agency's annual plan. AusTender does the same for federal work. A public tender for fence or deck repairs at a reserve or community facility is a signal a business can respond to through the stated process. Council planning permit registers show projects at application stage, which may include decks. Use aggregated permit activity to decide where to market. Do not use address data to contact individual owners, and do not turn up at a home to make an offer.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you came to know about the need, makes one observation that you can verify from a public notice or the business's own material, and offers one small next step, such as a written inspection of a defined area or a fifteen-minute call. The ACCC's July 2026 release on unsolicited selling reported many pressured or misleading approaches, and that about 80 per cent of respondents said unsolicited selling seldom gave useful information or offers. A specific, honest, named approach is a practical advantage.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide the follow-ups in advance. One reminder after a week and one final message two weeks later, then a pause, is a common pattern. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced paid work.

procedure: Write the deck and fence work, area, job-size and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and a source.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and record the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the licence and permit rules for the state and council before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A deck and fence operator covers three suburbs in Victoria. A public tender for timber fence repairs at a council reserve in one of them is posted on Buying for Victoria, with a closing date. The scenario is illustrative.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the operator respond, and what should the response contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: A published tender is a route the agency has opened, so responding through the stated process is appropriate. Before responding, the operator confirms the scope, his capacity and the deadline. He checks whether any of the work needs a council permit, because the permit position varies by council. He checks that each task is inside his licence and insurance. His response names the tender, says how he found it, offers one defined section of fence with an itemised price basis, and asks one question about access. He does not contact individual council staff through private contact details, and he does not pressure the council.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit, status, source and date columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact, such as an owner's address from a permit register.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that needs a permit or licence you do not hold.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence, insurance and council permit position before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or permit-dependent service in outreach unless you hold the licence the state requires and the council permit position is checked. Licence rules differ between states, and council permit rules differ between councils. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

A public listing or public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's direct-marketing guidance says public information is not exempt. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop when someone objects.

Telemarketing to numbers on the Do Not Call Register is limited to weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm, and not on Sundays or public holidays. That is from a 2018 industry guide, so check for updates before calling.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned
summary: Define the deck and fence work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
Any business with a website, because it probably spends money on services
A strata manager with several common-area decks inside your service area that you already visit

knowledgeChecks.question: A public tender for fence repairs at a council reserve is posted. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Message the council staff members at their private addresses
Respond through the tender process, after checking scope, capacity, deadline, licence and any permit need
Turn up at the reserve and offer to start the work the same day

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Ask the prospect to like your social media page first
Choose a fun subject line and keep the message short
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
